scope: All eight articles listed on the English articles index; paraphrased analytical synthesis

articles.title: Familiar vs Novel
synthesis: Familiar interaction models transfer learning and reduce the cost of initial use.
Novel interaction is defensible for meaningful differentiation, genuinely new capability or intentional exploration.
Even beneficial novelty must be validated with the intended audience rather than treated as self-evidently better.
articles.operational_rule: For routine interactions, start with conventions. For deliberately novel work, document the user benefit, fallback/learning path, and first-use study.
articles.counterexample: A story-driven exploratory experience can use unconventional scrolling; a checkout should rarely require it.

articles.title: Onboarding for Active Users
synthesis: Blocking introductory tours interrupt users who want to start a real task.
Contextual help, progressive introduction, starter templates and low-risk practice shift teaching to the moment of need.
Onboarding should support different paths and revisits, not require a single predetermined tutorial.
articles.operational_rule: Make the first meaningful action available immediately; show optional learning aids at the point of friction and evaluate time to first value.
articles.counterexample: A mandatory disclosure for legal consent cannot be deferred like an optional feature tour.

articles.title: Tesler’s Law
synthesis: An unavoidable amount of task complexity must be managed by the product team or its users.
Progressive disclosure reduces interface demand when secondary details remain accessible.
Automated defaults, prefilling and natural-language interaction can shift burden from users to the system, but assumptions must remain inspectable.
articles.operational_rule: List required domain decisions separately from implementation-driven chores. Automate chores; make domain decisions transparent and reversible where feasible.
articles.counterexample: Hiding calculated fees or inferred identity in a simplified checkout transfers risk, not just complexity.

articles.title: UX Psychology: Google Search
synthesis: A focused entry surface can eliminate irrelevant choices until users begin a task.
After initiation, additional filters and controls become relevant and can be progressively introduced.
Keeping the query visible reduces memory dependence; clear result grouping and fast feedback improve scan and iteration.
articles.operational_rule: Audit start, refinement and results separately: one obvious entry action; persistent context; scannable results; responsive feedback.
articles.counterexample: Stripping filtering options from a results page can slow exploration even if the homepage becomes cleaner.

articles.title: Peak-End Rule
synthesis: Remembered experience is strongly shaped by emotionally intense and final moments, not simply average screen quality.
Journey maps help identify anxiety, uncertainty and high-stakes transitions.
Transparent waits, recoverable errors and a clear completion state can reduce negative peaks; delight is secondary to correctness.
articles.operational_rule: Map each significant user journey with emotional peaks, breakpoints and completion. Fix failure/recovery before adding celebratory detail.
articles.counterexample: A delightful success animation does not compensate for silent data loss earlier in the task.

articles.title: The Psychology of Design
synthesis: Hick, Miller and Jakob support focused choices, meaningful chunking and conventional interaction, not numerical menu limits.
Mental-model mismatch is a serious risk in redesigns; transitions and user validation matter.
Psychological insights can be manipulative; user well-being and goal outcomes should outrank engagement for its own sake.
articles.operational_rule: Require benefit-to-user and non-manipulation checks when using behavioral nudges, scarcity, urgency, friction or habit mechanisms.
articles.counterexample: Maximizing time-in-product by slowing task completion is contrary to user-centered UX.

articles.title: Designing with Occam’s Razor
synthesis: Reducing unsupported assumptions and gratuitous interface elements prevents avoidable complexity.
Critique and removal are productive only when capabilities and clarity survive.
Novel layout flourishes and hidden navigation may appear minimal yet impose higher cognitive cost.
articles.operational_rule: For every element and step, ask what user job it does and what evidence justifies it. Remove only what does not serve a real job.
articles.counterexample: An unlabelled icon bar is visually minimal but cognitively expensive.

articles.title: Design Principles for Reducing Cognitive Load
synthesis: Unnecessary choices, thought and ambiguity are common sources of extraneous cognitive load.
Familiar design, readable content, intelligent defaults and reducing redundant tasks often outperform cosmetic simplification.
Choices must be visible as intelligible groups; hiding alternatives or using ambiguous icons can increase mental work.
articles.operational_rule: Measure recall, decision burden and findability; favor labels, contextual grouping, visible alternatives and clear task flow.
articles.counterexample: Moving needed options into undiscoverable menus simply exchanges visual clutter for search burden.
